caption:
Should you bring a filtered selfie to an aesthetic consultation? Yes—if you use it to explain your taste, not to diagnose your face.

A filter may reveal the proportion, contour, skin finish, or overall mood you prefer. But it can change several features at once and cannot map out a cosmetic treatment. If filtered images keep causing distress, pause the treatment conversation and seek support.

Circle the one change you actually like and use the screenshot to begin a more specific conversation. Save this for consultation day.

General education only.

#InstagramFilters #FilteredSelfies #AestheticConsultation #BeautyStandards #KoreanAesthetics
first_comment: If you had to name just one thing your favorite filter changes — shape, proportion, skin finish, or expression — which is it? That one word is a better starting point than the whole screenshot.

slides.alt_text: Slide 1 of 6: A woman holds a transparent smoothed-face panel beside her own. Title: Should you bring a filter to a consult?
Slide 2 of 6: Four blocks: softer, sharper, brighter, more balanced. A filter reveals your taste, not your diagnosis.
Slide 3 of 6: Four outlined tiles, jaw, nose, eyes and texture, each with a plus. Real treatment has no global slider.
Slide 4 of 6: Four blocks: shape, proportion, skin finish, expression. Headline: Name the thing you actually like.
Slide 5 of 6: Three numbered questions: What changed? What still feels like me? Is this image making me feel worse?
Slide 6 of 6: Use a filter as a clue, not instructions: one image, one detail you like, one question about what is realistic.
